sections.title: What does one radian measure?
sections.label: Units
sections.intro: Measure the short curved distance between the radii. If that distance equals the radius, the central angle is one radian.

blocks.html: The fraction of one revolution is \(\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\). A half-turn is \(\pi\text{ rad}=180^\circ\).

blocks.prompt:
A scanner arm of length \(17\) cm rotates about one end through \(90^\circ\).

Convert the rotation to radians.
blocks.hint: Multiply the number of degrees by π divided by 180.
blocks.solution:
One half-turn is \(180^\circ=\pi\text{ rad}\). Multiply \(90^\circ\) by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\), then simplify.

sections.title: How do I convert without mixing the factors?
sections.label: Convert
sections.intro: Start from the half-turn relation. Split the half-turn into as many equal steps as needed.

sections.title: What changes after one complete revolution?
sections.label: Turns
sections.intro: A turning object can rotate more than once. The final pointing direction repeats every revolution, but the distance travelled keeps increasing.

blocks.html: Reduce by \(2\pi\) only when the question asks for direction within one full turn.

examples.title: Measuring a turn in two units
examples.question:
A scanner arm of length \(16\) cm rotates about one end through \(72^\circ\).

  1. Convert the rotation to radians.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact length of the arc traced on the rim.

    [2]

  3. Find the angle in radians for the rest of the full circle.

    [2]
solution: (a) One half-turn is \(180^\circ=\pi\text{ rad}\). Multiply \(72^\circ\) by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\), then simplify.
(b) Use the angle in radians in \(s=r\theta\). The radius is \(16\) cm.
(c) A complete turn is \(2\pi\). Subtract the given angle from this total.

examples.title: Tracking repeated rotations
examples.question:
A control knob of radius \(10\) cm turns through \(45^\circ\) at each of \(4\) identical movements in the same direction.

  1. Find the total angle turned, in radians.

    [2]

  2. Find the total distance moved by a point on the rim.

    [2]

  3. Find the least non-negative angle giving the same final direction, in radians.

    [2]
solution: (a) The total before any reduction is \(180\) degrees. Convert this by multiplying by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\).
(b) The point travels the arc for each movement, including any complete turns.
Multiply the total angle in radians by \(10\).
(c) Each whole turn is \(2\pi\). Remove \(0\) complete turns.

sections.title: How does the angle determine the arc length?
sections.label: Arc
sections.intro: The larger the turn, the further a point on the rim travels. For a fixed radius, doubling the angle doubles the arc length.

blocks.html: An angle of \(\theta\) radians gives arc length \(s=r\theta\). The result uses the same length unit as the radius.

figure.alt: Sector AOB with central angle theta, radius r and an arc
figure.caption: Only the arc follows the circular boundary. The straight sides are the two radii.

blocks.prompt:
A curved edge joins the ends of two \(28\) cm radii. The angle at the centre is \(\frac{1}{4}\pi\) radians.

Find the length of the curved edge.
blocks.hint: Use s = rθ.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the radius \(28\) by the given radian angle.

\(7\pi\) cm.

blocks.html: An angle in degrees must be converted before using the formula.

sections.title: Which pieces belong to a sector perimeter?
sections.label: Boundary
sections.intro: Trace the boundary with your finger. Begin at the centre, move along one radius, trace the arc, and come back along the other radius.

blocks.html: The perimeter is \(P=2r+r\theta\). If perimeter is given, subtract both radii to find the arc.

blocks.prompt:
A complete sector boundary of radius \(32\) cm has perimeter \(64+\frac{96}{5}\pi\) cm.

Find the exact angle at the centre, in radians.
blocks.hint: Subtract both radii and then use the arc length formula.
blocks.solution:
The radii contribute \(64\) cm to the perimeter. The arc therefore has length \(\frac{96}{5}\pi\) cm.

Divide the arc length by \(32\).

\(\frac{3}{5}\pi\) rad.

blocks.html: The arc formula gives the curved piece only.

sections.title: Can two different sectors have the same arc length?
sections.label: Compare
sections.intro: A larger circle needs a smaller angle to sweep the same distance along its circumference.

blocks.html: With the arc length fixed, \(\theta=s/r\). Both arcs must use the same length unit before their sizes are compared.

blocks.prompt:
A sector of radius \(21\) cm has angle \(\frac{7}{4}\pi\) radians. A second circle of radius \(24\) cm has an arc of equal length.

Find the angle subtended by the arc on the second circle.
blocks.hint: Find the common arc length and divide by the second radius.
blocks.solution:
The common arc length is \(\frac{147}{4}\pi\) cm.

Divide it by the second radius, \(24\) cm.

\(\frac{49}{32}\pi\) rad.

blocks.html: An equal arc length does not imply an equal angle.

examples.title: From an arc to the whole sector edge
examples.question:
A curved edge joins the ends of two \(27\) cm radii. The angle at the centre is \(\frac{1}{6}\pi\) radians.

  1. Find the length of the curved edge.

    [2]

  2. Find the length of the remaining arc of the same circle.

    [2]

  3. Find the perimeter of a sector with the original angle and a radius \(16\) cm longer.

    [2]
solution: (a) Multiply the radius \(27\) by the given radian angle.
(b) The remaining sector angle is \(\frac{11}{6}\pi\) radians.
Keep the centre and radius fixed as you use \(s=r\theta\) again.
(c) The larger sector has radius \(43\) cm and still subtends the original angle.
Add both new radial sides and its longer arc.

examples.title: The same arc length on different circles
examples.question:
A sector of radius \(20\) cm has angle \(\frac{3}{2}\pi\) radians. A second circle of radius \(23\) cm has an arc of equal length.

  1. Find the angle subtended by the arc on the second circle.

    [3]

  2. Find the perimeter of the sector associated with the second arc.

    [2]

  3. Explain why the angle is smaller on the second circle.

    [1]
solution: (a) The common arc length is \(30\pi\) cm.
Divide it by the second radius, \(23\) cm.
(b) The sector edge uses the given arc and the two new radii.
(c) With \(s\) fixed, \(\theta=s/r\) decreases as the radius increases.
For a fixed arc length, the angle is inversely proportional to radius.

addmaths-0606-circular-areas-of-sectors.description: Find sector areas and recover missing quantities from an arc or an area.

sections.title: Why does the radius appear twice in the area formula?
sections.label: Area
sections.intro: The whole disc has area πr². A sector occupies the fraction of its turn measured in radians divided by a full turn.

blocks.html: This gives \(A=\frac12r^2\theta\), with the result in square units.

figure.alt: Sector AOB with central angle theta, radius r and an arc
figure.caption: Only the arc follows the circular boundary. The straight sides are the two radii.

blocks.prompt:
A sector has radius \(26\) cm and angle \(\frac{11}{12}\pi\) radians.

Find the exact area of the sector.
blocks.hint: Use half the radius squared times the radian angle.
blocks.solution:
A fraction \(\frac{11}{24}\) of the complete circle is used.

Equivalently, replace the radius and radian angle in \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\).

\(\frac{1859}{6}\pi\) cm².

blocks.html: The radius is squared even if the answer involves a fraction of pi.

blocks.prompt:
A sector has radius \(30\) cm and angle \(\frac{5}{4}\pi\) radians.

Find the exact area of the sector.
blocks.hint: Use half the radius squared times the radian angle.
blocks.solution:
A fraction \(\frac{5}{8}\) of the complete circle is used.

Equivalently, replace the radius and radian angle in \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\).

\(\frac{1125}{2}\pi\) cm².

blocks.html: Check that a half-turn gives half the area of a disc.

sections.title: How can a known area give a radius?
sections.label: Inverse
sections.intro: Rearrange to isolate the square of the radius. The radius itself represents a positive length.

blocks.html: Use \(r=\sqrt{\frac{2A}{\theta}}\) when the angle and area are known.

blocks.prompt:
A circular sector has area \(\frac{1078}{3}\pi\) cm² and angle \(\frac{11}{12}\pi\) radians.

Find the radius of the circle.
blocks.hint: Isolate the square of the radius and take the positive square root.
blocks.solution:
Rearrange \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\) to give \(r^2=\frac{2A}{\theta}\).

The factors of pi cancel to give \(r^2=784\). Choose the positive radius.

\(28\) cm.

blocks.html: The radius is not twice the area divided by the angle. That gives the radius squared.

blocks.prompt:
A circular sector has area \(640\pi\) cm² and angle \(\frac{5}{4}\pi\) radians.

Find the radius of the circle.
blocks.hint: Isolate the square of the radius and take the positive square root.
blocks.solution:
Rearrange \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\) to give \(r^2=\frac{2A}{\theta}\).

The factors of pi cancel to give \(r^2=1024\). Choose the positive radius.

\(32\) cm.

blocks.html: Keep all factors of pi until they can cancel algebraically.

sections.title: What if I know only the arc length and area?
sections.label: Combine
sections.intro: Compare the arc and area equations. Both contain the radius times the angle, so replace that product by the arc length.

blocks.html: Using \(s=r\theta\) gives \(A=\frac12rs\). Recover the radius before using the original formulas.

blocks.prompt:
The curved boundary of a sector is \(\frac{31}{6}\pi\) cm long. Its area is \(\frac{961}{12}\pi\) cm².

Find the radius of the sector.
blocks.hint: Combine the area and arc formulae to eliminate the angle.
blocks.solution:
Replace \(r\theta\) by \(s\) in \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\). Then \(r=\frac{2A}{s}\).

Divide twice the area by the given arc length to obtain \(31\) cm.

\(31\) cm.

blocks.html: The second equation uses the curved arc length, not the sector perimeter.

blocks.prompt:
The curved boundary of a sector is \(\frac{35}{3}\pi\) cm long. Its area is \(\frac{1225}{6}\pi\) cm².

Find the radius of the sector.
blocks.hint: Combine the area and arc formulae to eliminate the angle.
blocks.solution:
Replace \(r\theta\) by \(s\) in \(A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta\). Then \(r=\frac{2A}{s}\).

Divide twice the area by the given arc length to obtain \(35\) cm.

\(35\) cm.

blocks.html: One of the two equations should lose its angle when you combine them.

examples.question:

  1. Find the exact area of the sector.

Why does the radius appear twice in the area formula?

This gives \(A=\frac12r^2\theta\), with the result in square units.

How can a known area give a radius?

Use \(r=\sqrt{\frac{2A}{\theta}}\) when the angle and area are known.

A ring sector lies between radii \(11\) cm and \(27\) cm, with central angle \(\frac{1}{4}\pi\) radians.

  1. Find the exact area of the ring sector.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact perimeter of the ring sector.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact difference between the lengths of the two arcs.

    [2]
solution: (a) The sectors have the same angle. Subtract the smaller one, using \(A=\frac{1}{2}\theta(R^2-r^2)\) for their difference.
(b) The outer and inner arcs total \(\frac{19}{2}\pi\) cm.
Each straight edge has length \(16\) cm.
(c) The shared angle is \(\frac{1}{4}\pi\) radians. The two radii differ by \(16\) cm.

examples.title: Follow the outer boundary
examples.question:
A running track consists of a rectangle of straight length \(10\) m and width \(14\) m, with a semicircle added to each shorter edge.

  1. Find the exact outer perimeter.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact area enclosed.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact increase in area if each straight section is lengthened by 4 m with the same width.

    [2]
solution: (a) The two straight parts have total length \(20\) m. Together the two semicircles contribute the circumference of a circle of radius \(7\) m.
(b) The rectangular area is \(140\) m². Combine the two semicircular areas into \(49\pi\) m².
(c) The two semicircles are unchanged. A rectangular strip 4 m long is added.

examples.title: The gap between two tangents and an arc
examples.question:
A circle has centre \(O\) and radius \(14\) cm. The tangents at \(A\) and \(B\) meet at \(T\). The smaller angle \(AOB\) is \(\frac{2}{3}\pi\) radians.

  1. Find the exact length of \(AT\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact area of quadrilateral \(OATB\).

    [2]

  3. Find the exact area bounded by the two tangent segments and the minor arc \(AB\).

    [3]
solution: (a) The radius meets the tangent at a right angle. The line \(OT\) bisects angle \(AOB\) because the two right triangles have a common hypotenuse and equal radii.
Use \(AT=r\tan(\theta/2)\).
(b) Its two congruent right triangles each have area \(\frac12 r\cdot AT\). Add them.
(c) The minor sector uses angle \(\frac{2}{3}\pi\) and has area \(\frac{196}{3}\pi\) cm².
Subtract this sector from the full quadrilateral.

revision.body:
Where are the two radii used in a ring sector?

Subtract to get \(A=\frac12\theta(R^2-r^2)\). Its straight edges each have length \(R-r\).

How can I tell which edges remain outside?

Use the straight lengths and arcs on the outline for perimeter. Split the interior into non-overlapping shapes for area.

Which areas enclose a gap between tangents?

Use the area of the right triangles formed by radii and tangents. Subtract the appropriate sector to isolate the gap.

examples.title: Two equal circles and their shared region
examples.question:
Two circles have equal radius \(33\) cm. Each centre lies on the other circle. The common chord has endpoints \(A\) and \(B\).

  1. Find the angle subtended by the shorter arc AB at either centre.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact perimeter of the region inside both circles.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact area of the region inside both circles.

    [3]
solution: (a) Join the two centres to \(A\) and to \(B\). This forms an equilateral triangle on each side of the centre line.
Each gives \(\frac{1}{3}\pi\) radians at a centre. Add the two angles.
(b) Each boundary arc has length \(22\pi\) cm. The complete outline has two such arcs.
(c) Each half of the lens is a minor segment with sector area \(363\pi\) cm².
The triangle for each segment contributes \(\frac{1089}{4}\sqrt{3}\) cm².
Subtract one triangle from each sector and add the two identical segments.

examples.title: Change the radius and keep the area fixed
examples.question:
The perimeter of a sector with radius \(20\) cm is \(40+5\pi\) cm. A second sector has the same area but radius \(25\) cm.

  1. Find the exact central angle of the first sector.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact area of either sector.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact angle of the second sector.

    [2]
solution: (a) The curved edge has length \(5\pi\) cm after removing both radial sides.
Divide this arc length by the original radius \(20\) cm.
(b) Use the angle and radius of the original sector. The area is preserved by the change.
(c) The second squared radius is \(\frac{25}{16}\) times the first.
To keep \(r^2\theta\) fixed, multiply the first angle by \(\frac{16}{25}\).
